lessons.title: Medieval warfare: knights, archers and the feudal army c1250–c1500

before.content_html:
An Army Built on Land and Loyalty

Between c1250 and c1500 the English army was not a paid, full-time force. It was a feudal host — a temporary army summoned by the king from his lords, who in turn brought their tenants. Society and command were one and the same: the king led the great lords, the lords led the knights, and the knights led the foot soldiers from their estates. Knight service meant that a lord who held land from the king owed roughly 40 days of military service each year — on horseback, fully armed.

A medieval English army therefore had three layers. At the top sat the mounted knight, the most expensive and prestigious soldier on the field. Below him stood the foot infantry — spearmen and men-at-arms drawn from yeomen and tenants. And from the late thirteenth century, archers became the third pillar, as kings realised that ranged firepower could decide a battle before the cavalry charged.

Key Fact

A medieval English army was raised through feudal duty: the king summoned lords, who brought knights, who brought their tenants. The three main components were the mounted knight, the infantry and the archer.

The Mounted Knight — and Why He Started to Decline

A fully equipped knight cost as much as a small village. He needed mail armour (later plate), a war horse, lance, sword and a long apprenticeship. On the battlefield he charged shoulder-to-shoulder, hoping to break the enemy line by sheer weight and shock. Against unprepared infantry this was devastating. Against well-organised foot soldiers with the right weapons, it was suicidal.

At Falkirk in 1298, Scottish foot soldiers formed schiltrons — tight rings of pike-points like a hedgehog — and English knights could not break them. The ring was eventually destroyed not by horsemen but by English longbowmen who shot the schiltrons apart from a safe distance. The same pattern was repeated at Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415): mounted French knights charged across muddy ground into a wall of arrows. The mounted knight remained socially dominant, but militarily he was already in retreat.

The Longbow Revolution

The longbow was around six feet tall and required a draw weight of 100–150 lb — far heavier than a modern hunting bow. A trained archer could shoot ten or twelve arrows a minute and reach 250 yards. Edward III made longbow practice compulsory by law, and Sunday archery became a legal obligation in every village. By Agincourt (1415), perhaps 80% of an English army was longbowmen.

The longbow was decisive because it was cheap, fast and used by men of low status. A peasant with two pence worth of yew and a quiver could kill a knight worth two hundred pounds. This challenged the social logic of the feudal host, where battlefield power was supposed to mirror landowning rank. Wars now turned on what large numbers of trained commoners could do.

Tudor and Victorian writers loved the story of plucky English archers single-handedly destroying French chivalry. Modern scholars (Anne Curry of Southampton, the Royal Armouries) point out that the longbow worked alongside funnel terrain, deep mud, French command failures and Henry V’s decision to fight on a narrow front between two woods. The longbow was crucial — but it was one factor among several. Examiners reward students who weigh weapons against terrain and leadership rather than crediting one cause alone.

Schiltrons, Pikes and Other Foot Formations

The schiltron was a Scottish answer to mounted knights, but it was not the only foot formation that mattered. The men-at-arms — the heavily armoured swordsmen of knightly rank — increasingly fought dismounted. At Agincourt the English knights got off their horses, drove sharpened stakes into the ground and stood with the archers. The horseback charge was becoming an option, not the default.

Gunpowder Arrives

From the early fourteenth century, English armies used gunpowder in primitive cannon. Edward III deployed small bombards at Crécy in 1346. By the fifteenth century, large siege guns were knocking down castle walls that had stood for centuries. At the siege of Constantinople (1453), Ottoman cannon ended the medieval city defence. In England, Henry VIII’s gun foundries laid the basis of artillery that would change war for good in the next century.

Cannon did not yet dominate the open battlefield — they were slow, heavy and unreliable in 1400. But they ended the supremacy of the high stone wall, which had defined siege warfare for a thousand years. Combined with the longbow, gunpowder squeezed the mounted knight from two sides: cheap missile troops broke up cavalry charges, and cannon broke the castle that had been the knight’s refuge.

Students writing about the Western Front sometimes call trench warfare an invention of the twentieth century. The basic ideas — ditches, earthworks, layered defensive lines — are far older. Castle ditches, the prepared ground at Agincourt, and later the field fortifications of the New Model Army all use the same logic. What changed in 1914 was the machine gun, the artillery shell and the railway, not the digging. Across this whole unit you should look for continuity in tactics even when weapons change.

Key Fact

By 1500 the longbow had broken the mounted knight on the battlefield, and gunpowder cannon had begun to break the castle walls he sheltered behind. Both weapons let trained commoners challenge a noble warrior class.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the longbow became the dominant English missile weapon by c1415.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• It outranged and outpaced earlier missile weapons: a 100–150 lb draw weight delivered up to ten arrows a minute at 250 yards.
• Edward III made longbow practice compulsory through law, requiring Sunday archery in every village — by 1415 trained archers were available in large numbers.
• It was cheap and used by commoners: a yew bow and quiver cost a fraction of a knight's equipment, so kings could field thousands of archers.
• Battles such as Falkirk (1298) and the French wars demonstrated its power against schiltrons and against mounted knights, encouraging further reliance on it.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content.

Indicative content — arguments supporting science/technology as most important:
• The longbow gave trained commoners decisive battlefield firepower at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415).
• The arrival of gunpowder and primitive cannon (Crécy 1346, Constantinople 1453) ended the high stone wall as a guarantee of safety.
• Better armour (plate), saddles and horse breeding all changed the cost and the role of the mounted knight.
• Improvements in shipbuilding and missile weaponry shaped how England fought across the Channel.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors (governments and individuals; attitudes in society):
• Government action was decisive: Edward III's compulsory archery law made the longbow available in mass numbers; Henry V's decisions at Agincourt turned a weapon into a victory.
• The feudal host was a social institution as much as a military one — knight service, the obligation to serve 40 days, was a legal/political fact, not a technology.
• Attitudes in society — the chivalric ideal, the prestige of the mounted knight — slowed the decline of cavalry even after the longbow had made it tactically vulnerable.
• Without organised muster, billeting and royal taxation to pay archers and gunners, the new weapons could not have been used effectively.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs technology against governments/individuals/attitudes, uses accurate period detail (longbow, knight service, Crécy, Agincourt) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

lessons.title: Falkirk 1298 and Agincourt 1415: medieval battles and their leaders

before.content_html:
Two Battles, One Argument

Falkirk (1298) and Agincourt (1415) sit at either end of the medieval period and tell the same story from two angles. At Falkirk an English king crushed a Scottish foot army by combining knights and archers. At Agincourt an English king defeated a French knightly army by relying on archers and dismounted men-at-arms. Together they show why the longbow archer became the deciding figure on the medieval battlefield, and why combined arms was already a real idea long before the modern era.

Key Fact

At Falkirk (1298) Edward I defeated William Wallace by using longbowmen to break the Scottish schiltrons. At Agincourt (1415) Henry V used longbowmen and dismounted men-at-arms to destroy a much larger French army.

Falkirk, 22 July 1298 — The First Time the Longbow Decided a Battle

William Wallace had won at Stirling Bridge a year earlier by trapping an English army on a narrow crossing. Now Edward I was determined to fight on his own terms. He brought a large army northwards: heavy cavalry, men-at-arms, and crucially around two thousand Welsh and English longbowmen.

Wallace formed his foot soldiers into four schiltrons — tightly packed circles of pikemen presenting outward-pointing 12-foot spears. Cavalry could not ride into them. Edward’s knights charged anyway and were repulsed. Then Edward did something new: he pulled the cavalry back and ordered his longbowmen forward. The arrows tore the schiltrons apart from a safe distance. Once the rings broke, the cavalry rode through the gaps and the Scottish foot army was massacred. Wallace escaped, but his military reputation was destroyed.

Falkirk mattered because of field of fire. The schiltron was effective only as long as the enemy stayed in front of pikepoints. As soon as ranged weapons could safely shoot from outside spear-reach, the formation became a death trap. Edward I had stumbled onto a basic principle of all later medieval warfare: combined arms beats any single troop type.

Agincourt, 25 October 1415 — The Lesson Repeated

A century later Henry V faced the same problem in reverse. He had landed in Normandy with around 12,000 men but his army was reduced by dysentery and the long march; by the time he reached Agincourt in Picardy he had perhaps 6,000 fighting men. Most of them were longbowmen. The French had assembled a far larger army — estimates range from 12,000 to 25,000 — including thousands of mounted knights eager to wipe out the English invader.

Henry chose his ground carefully. He fought in a narrow funnel of recently ploughed field between two woods, soaked by autumn rain. The French could not deploy their numbers; mud trapped horses and armoured men. The English longbowmen drove sharpened wooden stakes into the ground in front of their positions. The dismounted English men-at-arms stood between the archers as a steady, slow-moving line.

When the French knights charged, the longbowmen released arrows in massed flights. Horses fell in the mud. Knights pressed forward on foot through ploughed earth in 60 lb of plate armour. The first French line crashed into the English line exhausted. Behind them, more French knights kept arriving and trampling the wounded. By the end of the day the French had lost thousands of nobles; English casualties were a few hundred. The longbow had again decided a battle — but only because Henry had picked the field, the timing and the formation.

Tudor and Victorian retellings made Agincourt a story of plucky English archers and effete French nobles. Modern scholars (Anne Curry of Southampton, the Royal Armouries, Juliet Barker) emphasise the muddy ground, the funnel terrain, French command failures and Henry V’s decisions on dismounting and stake-driving. The longbow was crucial — but logistics, leadership and luck of weather all sat alongside it. Examiners reward students who weigh weapons against terrain and command rather than crediting one cause alone.

Logistics, Command and Morale

Both battles also turned on logistics. Edward I had marched a large, well-fed army into Scotland on prepared roads with supply trains. Wallace, by contrast, had been shadowing the English to deny them food, and his men were tiring. Henry V’s army had eaten badly for weeks and many were sick — but the French were also disorganised, with no overall commander, multiple grand lords competing for the right to fight in the front rank.

Command and morale sealed both outcomes. Wallace’s army began Falkirk demoralised after a year of evading battle, while Edward I had personally led his men since dawn. Henry V was famous for walking among his archers the night before Agincourt; Shakespeare invented many of the details, but the underlying point — that an English king physically present with his men was a force-multiplier — is real. The French at Agincourt had no such single voice: orders were ignored, ranks were jumbled and the rear pushed the front into the mud.

A schiltron worked by packing men shoulder to shoulder so that the spears formed a solid wall. To protect every direction the men had to stay in close formation — they could not fan out without losing the wall of points. Once English longbowmen began shooting from outside spear-reach, every Scottish soldier was a stationary target. Loosening the formation meant losing the protection from cavalry; staying tight meant being shot down. Falkirk shows the basic problem of any single-weapon system: it has to be supported by something else, or it can be cancelled by ranged fire.

Key Fact

Both battles show combined arms in action: Edward I used longbows to break the Scottish schiltrons before unleashing his cavalry, and Henry V used a narrow muddy funnel and sharpened stakes to channel French knights into massed arrow fire.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • At Falkirk (1298) Edward I’s longbowmen broke the Scottish schiltrons before his cavalry charged through the gaps — the first time the longbow decided a major battle.
  • At Agincourt (1415) Henry V used narrow funnel terrain, deep mud, sharpened stakes and dismounted men-at-arms to turn massed longbow fire into a crushing victory over a much larger French army.
  • Neither outcome was the longbow alone — combined arms, command, terrain and logistics all mattered. Examiners reward students who weigh several factors against each other.

lessons.title: Civilians and recruitment in the medieval army

before.content_html:
Recruitment by Duty, Not Choice

Between c1250 and c1500 the king did not pay a standing army. When he needed soldiers, he summoned them through the obligations of feudal society. The classic device was the feudal levy, sometimes called the feudal host. A great lord owed knight service to the king; a knight owed service to the lord; a tenant owed service to the knight on whose land he worked. War therefore travelled down through every level of medieval society, all the way to the village.

Within the village, men were summoned to a muster — a public assembly at which the local sheriff or steward inspected weapons, horses and physical fitness. The Assize of Arms (1252 and earlier versions) required every able-bodied freeman to keep arms appropriate to his wealth: a knight had to keep a war horse and full mail; a poor freeman might only owe a bow, knife and helmet. From the late thirteenth century, every village was expected to provide longbowmen for royal campaigns.

Key Fact

Medieval armies were raised by feudal duty, by the muster of armed freemen under the Assize of Arms, and (later) by indenture — written contracts in which lords promised to bring fixed numbers of men in return for cash.

Indentures and the Slow Move Towards Pay

By the fourteenth century, the simple feudal levy was creaking. Foreign campaigns — especially in France during the Hundred Years War — needed armies for far longer than the standard forty days. Edward III began to use the indenture — a written agreement in which a great lord promised to bring (say) 100 men-at-arms and 200 archers for six months at a fixed daily rate. Indentures were sealed in two halves, with each side keeping one as proof.

Indentured soldiers were often called ‘contract’ soldiers. They were not yet a standing army — they went home when the campaign ended — but they were paid, professional and used to fighting together. Henry V’s Agincourt army was raised this way: roughly 25 great captains contracted to bring fixed retinues. The indenture system also brought rougher elements into royal service: experienced veterans of earlier wars, foreign mercenaries and men attracted by pay rather than feudal loyalty.

Training: Sunday Archery and the Practice Field

Most medieval training was decentralised. Knights trained for years in their own households, learning sword, lance and horsemanship from boyhood. Men-at-arms trained in noble retinues. The longbow, however, required mass training across the kingdom — you could not raise 5,000 archers in a hurry.

Edward III therefore made longbow practice a legal duty. Sunday archery was compulsory in every village; football and other ‘wasteful’ games were banned by statute (1363) so that men spent their free time at the butts. Local bowyers and fletchers supplied bows and arrows. By the fifteenth century, England was unique in fielding tens of thousands of trained longbowmen drawn from the peasant and yeoman classes — a rare moment of large-scale, state-mandated training before the modern era.

Students often write that compulsion to serve in the British army began in 1916 with the Military Service Act. In fact, compulsory military service is much older. Feudal duty obliged tenants to serve when called; the Assize of Arms required freemen to keep weapons; later, county militia ballots and naval impressment kept compulsion alive into the nineteenth century. What changed in 1916 was the scale and the nationwide industrial-era machinery, not the principle. Examiner’s Reports reward students who can place 1916 on a long timeline of British military compulsion.

Civilians and the Cost of War

Medieval war pressed onto civilian life in three main ways. The first was purveyance — the king’s right to buy provisions for an army at fixed (often below market) prices. Royal officials descended on villages and seized grain, ale, livestock, carts and labour, leaving promises to pay later. In hard years this could starve a community.

The second was billeting. Soldiers on the march were quartered in private homes, ate the family’s food, slept in their beds and sometimes assaulted the householders. Towns near major campaign routes — Berwick on the Scottish border, Dover for the French wars — lived under almost permanent billeting. The unpopularity of billeting is one reason later kings worked to fund standing armies in barracks.

The third was chevauchée — mounted raids deep into enemy land, deliberately destroying farms, burning villages, slaughtering livestock and seizing valuables. English armies under Edward III and the Black Prince ran chevauchées across France. Civilians on the receiving end were ruined; soldiers and lords took home plunder that sometimes outpaced their pay.

Edward I’s Statute of Winchester (1285) tied military duty to local policing duty. Every freeman was required to keep arms by his wealth, and a parish constable was given the responsibility for raising the hue and cry. The same men who would form the muster for the king’s war were also expected to chase a thief through the village. Recruitment, training and law enforcement were therefore woven together. This is one reason the modern army and modern police force took so long to separate: in medieval England they were the same body of armed men, called out for different reasons.

Key Fact

Purveyance, billeting and the chevauchée show that medieval war squeezed civilians as much as soldiers. Royal officials seized grain, soldiers were quartered in private homes, and English raids across France enriched soldiers while ruining French villagers.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the medieval feudal levy.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• It was the system by which the king summoned soldiers from his lords in return for the land they held.
• Service was usually limited to about 40 days a year.
• It travelled all the way down the social ladder — lords brought knights, knights brought tenants from their estates.
• It was supplemented from the late thirteenth century by the muster, where freemen presented themselves armed under the Assize of Arms.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to medieval recruitment without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why English kings began to use indentures to raise armies in the fourteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The 40-day limit of feudal service was too short for foreign campaigns: Edward III's wars in France in the 1340s and 1350s needed soldiers for many months at a time.
• Indentures gave kings predictable numbers — a contract specified, for example, 100 men-at-arms and 200 archers for six months.
• Paid, contracted soldiers tended to be more experienced and better trained than reluctant feudal levies serving out their forty days.
• Indentures could be sealed with the great captains in advance of a campaign, allowing the crown to plan logistics and pay rates in detail.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (Hundred Years War, 40-day limit, set ratios of men-at-arms to archers) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of indentures without explaining their introduction.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of compulsory longbow practice in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• Edward III made longbow practice a legal duty so that thousands of trained archers would be available when summoned.
• Sunday practice at the village butts was required, and 'wasteful' games such as football were banned by statute in 1363.
• Local bowyers and fletchers supplied bows and arrows so that even poor villagers could practise.
• It produced a unique English advantage — by the fifteenth century, no other country could field longbowmen in such numbers.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to archery without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of purveyance and billeting in the experience of medieval civilians during war.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Purveyance allowed royal officials to seize grain, livestock and carts at fixed prices below market value, often leaving only promises to pay — in bad harvests this could starve a village.
• Billeting forced ordinary households to provide food, beds and sometimes labour for soldiers on the march, with little protection against assault or theft.
• Both pressed onto civilian life regardless of feudal status — even free villagers had no legal way to refuse a royal officer or a billeting captain.
• Towns on major campaign routes (Berwick, Dover) faced near-constant disruption — these duties shaped attitudes towards royal taxation and standing armies for centuries.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (named towns, Assize of Arms, royal officers, harvest impact) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of civilian hardship without explaining the importance of purveyance and billeting.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the medieval chevauchée.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• A mounted raid deep into enemy territory aimed at destroying farms, villages and infrastructure.
• Deliberate slaughter of livestock and burning of crops to weaken the enemy economy and morale.
• Used extensively by Edward III and the Black Prince in France during the Hundred Years War.
• Plunder taken on the chevauchée was a major source of soldiers' income, sometimes outpacing pay.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to medieval raids without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
‘Recruitment in the medieval period was based mainly on duty rather than pay.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the feudal levy
• indentures.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content.

Indicative content — arguments for duty:
• The feudal levy summoned lords, knights and tenants in return for land — service, not wages.
• The Assize of Arms required freemen to keep weapons; the Statute of Winchester (1285) tied them to the village muster.
• Edward III's compulsory longbow practice forced training onto every village, regardless of pay.
• Foreign mercenary service was distrusted; English society in this period was structured around obligation, not employment.

Indicative content — arguments for pay:
• From the fourteenth century, indentures contracted lords to bring fixed numbers of men for fixed daily rates of pay — the start of paid soldiering on a large scale.
• Henry V's Agincourt army was raised this way through about 25 great captains.
• Plunder from the chevauchée was effectively informal pay; many soldiers fought for what they could take, not for feudal duty.
• The 40-day limit of feudal service was useless for long foreign wars, so cash had to play a role.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs duty against pay across the period, uses accurate period detail (feudal levy, Assize of Arms, indenture, chevauchée) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed.
Developing: One side developed more than the other; judgement is asserted rather than defended.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement.

lessons.title: Early modern warfare and the New Model Army c1500–c1700

before.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark causation-style or 16-mark judgement on Naseby, do not retell the battle. Pick two factors (Cromwell’s drill and the discipline of the Ironsides; the Self-Denying Ordinance and professionalisation; numbers; Rupert’s loss of control) and weigh them. Use specific period vocabulary — pike-and-shot, matchlock, Ironsides, regimental drill, free quarter, standing army — for SPaG. For 4-mark ‘Describe Two Features’, give two distinct features with one supporting detail each — do not slip into explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of pike-and-shot warfare in seventeenth-century England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• Musketeers and pikemen fought side by side in linked blocks, with the pikemen protecting the musketeers while they reloaded.
• A typical infantry regiment by the 1640s had roughly two musketeers for every pikeman.
• Pikemen carried 16–18 foot pikes and stood in tight formation to receive cavalry charges as a hedgehog of points.
• Musketeers fired matchlock muskets in volleys and then retired through gaps in the pike block to reload while another rank stepped forward.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to early modern warfare without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a standing army began to emerge in England between c1500 and c1700.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• New gunpowder weapons demanded long drilled training: musketeers and pikemen had to coordinate in volleys and pike blocks under fire — peasants summoned for a campaign could not learn this in a few weeks.
• Foreign campaigns and the Civil War (1642–1651) needed armies for years rather than 40 days, so paid contracts and standing forces were unavoidable.
• The New Model Army (1645) showed that a paid, drilled, nationally-administered army could destroy older volunteer forces — its lessons survived after the war.
• Charles II kept household regiments in pay after the Restoration of 1660, establishing the principle of a permanent army even though Parliament demanded annual Mutiny Acts.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (named regiments, named dates, the Self-Denying Ordinance, the Mutiny Act) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of armies without explaining the rise of a standing force.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the New Model Army.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• It was created in February 1645 as a single national Parliamentary army of around 22,000 men.
• It was paid regularly (when Parliament could find the money) and supplied through a national administration in London.
• Its officers were chosen for ability rather than inherited rank, after the Self-Denying Ordinance removed most aristocratic commanders.
• It was drilled to a uniform standard, with Cromwell's 'Ironsides' cavalry trained to rally after a charge rather than chase fugitives.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to the army without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Parliament won the Battle of Naseby in 1645.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Numbers: Fairfax and Cromwell had around 14,000 men against the Royalists' 7,500.
• Discipline of the Ironsides: Cromwell's cavalry rallied after their charge and turned inwards to attack the Royalist infantry, while Prince Rupert's Royalist horse rode off the field to plunder the Parliamentary baggage train.
• Drill and command: the New Model Army's officers were chosen for ability and the soldiers had practised regimental drill until manoeuvres were near-automatic — by contrast, Royalist coordination collapsed once Rupert was out of contact.
• Pay and morale: Parliamentary troops were paid and fed regularly; many Royalist regiments were owed wages and short of supply, weakening their willingness to stand.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (Ironsides, Rupert, Self-Denying Ordinance, named numbers) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Naseby without explaining the outcome.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of the English Civil War on civilians.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• Free quarter — soldiers ate at householders' tables and slept in their homes, leaving paper IOUs that often went unpaid.
• Forced requisition of horses, carts, fodder and food when armies marched through a region.
• Towns sacked when they refused to surrender — for example, after sieges in the West Country.
• Local conscription through Royalist commissions of array and Parliamentary militia ordinances pulled men away from farms and trades.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to suffering without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text:
‘The role of Oliver Cromwell was the main reason for the Parliamentary victory at Naseby in 1645.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Ironsides
• the New Model Army.

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement (with SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks.

Indicative content — arguments for Cromwell's role:
• Cromwell drilled the Ironsides specifically to rally after a charge and re-engage in formation, which was the decisive move at Naseby.
• His command of the Parliamentary right wing turned the cavalry battle into a flank attack on the Royalist infantry.
• His insistence on choosing officers by ability (the Self-Denying Ordinance) shaped the New Model Army that fought the battle.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Sir Thomas Fairfax was Lord General and overall commander; the army's organisation and choice of ground were his work.
• The New Model Army itself — paid, drilled, nationally administered, larger than the Royalist field army — gave Parliament a structural advantage that no individual commander created alone.
• Royalist failure: Prince Rupert's horse rode off the field to plunder, leaving the Royalist infantry exposed; this was a Royalist mistake as much as a Parliamentary success.
• Numbers: Fairfax and Cromwell fielded around 14,000 men against Charles I's 7,500.
• Pay and supply: regular Parliamentary pay produced steady morale that the Royalists could not match.

Mastering: Sustained, well-supported argument that weighs Cromwell against Fairfax, the New Model as a system and Royalist failures, uses accurate period detail (Ironsides, Self-Denying Ordinance, Rupert, named numbers) and reaches a clear, justified judgement signposted in the introduction and conclusion. SPaG: consistent accuracy with confident period vocabulary.
Secure: Both sides considered with relevant detail; judgement is present but less consistently developed. SPaG: mostly accurate.
Developing: One side dominates; judgement is asserted rather than defended. SPaG: inconsistent.
Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

lessons.title: Industrial warfare c1700–c1900: weapons, transport and the cavalry’s decline

before.content_html:
A Battlefield Transformed by Industry

Between roughly 1700 and 1900 the British army fought with weapons and supply systems that were unrecognisable from those of the New Model Army. The smoothbore musket gave way to the rifle. Cannon evolved into long-range field artillery. Horse-drawn supply trains were replaced by steam-powered railways and steamships. Each change had a battlefield consequence: men could be killed at greater distances, formations had to spread out, and the mounted knight — who had survived in the form of heavy cavalry — finally lost his role on the line. This lesson connects the technology to the change in tactics.

Key Fact

By 1900 the effective range of an infantry weapon had risen from about 75 yards (smoothbore musket, 1700) to around 1,000 yards (Lee-Metford rifle, 1888). Field artillery range rose from a few hundred yards to several miles. Soldiers had to spread out or be cut down.

From Smoothbore Musket to Rifle

The eighteenth-century British infantryman carried the ‘Brown Bess’ smoothbore smoothbore musket. It was unreliable beyond 75 yards, so commanders packed men shoulder to shoulder in three-deep lines and relied on volume of fire. By the 1850s the army was issuing the Pattern 1853 Enfield rifle, whose grooved barrel imparted spin to a hollow-based Minié ball. Rifling made an aimed shot possible at 600 yards. By the late 1880s the Lee-Metford was a magazine-fed bolt-action rifle firing smokeless powder — accurate, fast and concealed.

The tactical effect was huge. Infantry packed shoulder to shoulder were now massacred by the very weapons they themselves carried. Officers had to disperse their men into open order, use cover, and abandon the bright red lines of the eighteenth century. Smokeless powder also meant a soldier could no longer see who was firing at him — the ‘empty battlefield’ of the late nineteenth century had arrived.

Field Guns and Heavy Artillery

Cannon followed the same trajectory. Eighteenth-century smoothbore guns fired solid cannon balls a few hundred yards. By the second half of the nineteenth century rifled field artillery could throw explosive shells several miles. Breech-loading replaced muzzle-loading, dramatically raising rate of fire. By the Boer War (1899–1902) British and Boer guns were engaging each other across distances that would have been incomprehensible in 1815. Heavy artillery — siege guns and howitzers — specialised in flattening fortifications and trenches.

Mass production made this possible. Government armouries at Enfield Lock and private firms such as Armstrong and Vickers used interchangeable parts and steam-driven machine tools to turn out rifles and shells in numbers that earlier centuries could not have imagined. War was no longer just an event on a battlefield: it was an industrial output.

Trench-style earthworks are far older than the Western Front. Naseby (1645) was fought from prepared field positions. Wellington’s Lines of Torres Vedras (1810) ran for over 50 km of ditches and forts. The American Civil War siege of Petersburg (1864–65) was nine months of trench warfare. By the 1880s a soldier under accurate rifle and shell fire had no choice but to dig in. The 1914–18 Western Front industrialised what already existed; it did not invent it. Examiners reward students who recognise this continuity rather than treating the trenches as a sudden 1914 invention.

Steam, Railways and the Logistics Revolution

Industrial weapons demanded industrial supply. Steam logistics reshaped how wars were fought. The Crimean War (1854–56) saw Britain ship an entire army to the Black Sea coast by steamer; once there a small railway was built from Balaclava harbour up to the siege lines at Sevastopol to carry shells and food. By the Boer War, British troops, horses and stores moved across South Africa on rail networks that the Boer commandos in turn tried to sabotage.

The telegraph went with the railway. From the 1850s a commander in London could send orders to a general in the field within hours, not weeks. War correspondents (covered in the next lesson) used the same wires to file reports for the morning’s newspapers. Industrialisation collapsed not just battlefield distance but the political distance between government, public and front line.

The mounted heavy cavalryman had been a battlefield decider for nearly a thousand years. By 1900 he was almost obsolete. Rifled bullets cut horses down at 600 yards. Field artillery saturated open ground with shrapnel. Smokeless powder meant cavalry could not see the riflemen firing at them. The Crimean War already showed the cost of the old role — the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava (1854) lost roughly 40 per cent of its men in twenty minutes against Russian guns. By the Boer War, cavalry survived only as mounted infantry — troops who rode to the fight, dismounted and used rifles. The grand cavalry charge had become suicidal.

Industrialised Supply: A New Kind of War

Industrialised supply is the thread tying weapons and transport together. A regiment in 1815 carried lead, wadding and powder into a battle that lasted a day. A regiment in 1899 needed millions of brass cartridges, thousands of artillery shells, refrigerated meat and condensed milk — all delivered by railhead. War became a competition between economies as much as between armies. The pattern set in the long nineteenth century is the pattern that runs straight on into the world wars: whichever side could produce, transport and replace at industrial speed had the advantage.

Key Fact

Three changes drove the transformation: rifled bullets gave infantry a 600-yard reach; rifled breech-loading artillery threw shells for miles; steam railways and ships moved armies and supplies faster than horses ever could. Together they ended the close-order line and the cavalry charge.
before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain Why’ on weapons or transport in this period, examiners want two clearly separate reasons, each developed with specific named detail (Minié ball, Enfield rifle, Lee-Metford, rifled field gun, the Balaclava railway, Torres Vedras). Avoid the trap of describing one weapon at length — instead pick two factors and link both back to the question. For 4-mark ‘Describe Two Features’, name the feature plus one supporting fact (e.g. ‘rifling — spiral grooves spinning the bullet for accuracy out to 600 yards’). Use period vocabulary throughout for SPaG: rifling, breech-loading, smokeless powder, steam logistics.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Pattern 1853 Enfield rifle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• It had a rifled (grooved) barrel that imparted spin to the bullet, making accurate fire possible at around 600 yards.
• It used the Minié ball — a conical lead bullet with a hollow base that expanded into the rifling on firing.
• It was muzzle-loaded but produced in large numbers at the Royal Small Arms Factory at Enfield Lock using interchangeable parts.
• It was the standard British infantry weapon of the Crimean War (1854–56) and remained in service for around a decade.

practice_questions.text: Explain why infantry tactics changed in the second half of the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Rifling and the Minié ball pushed accurate small-arms range from around 75 yards (smoothbore musket) to 600 yards, making close-order shoulder-to-shoulder lines suicidal.
• Breech-loading rifled field artillery threw explosive shells at far longer range and higher rate of fire than smoothbore cannon, saturating open ground with shrapnel.
• Smokeless powder (from the 1880s) hid the firer, producing the ‘empty battlefield’ in which dispersed open order, cover and concealment replaced massed volleys.
• Mass production at Enfield Lock and firms like Armstrong and Vickers meant every soldier could carry industrial-quality weapons, so both sides had the same lethal reach.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the heavy cavalry charge declined as a battlefield tactic in the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Rifled small arms could now hit horses and riders accurately at 600 yards, so cavalry were cut down before reaching enemy lines — shown by the casualties of the Light Brigade at Balaclava (1854).
• Breech-loading rifled field artillery saturated open ground with shrapnel, making the open approach a cavalry charge requires effectively impassable.

• By the Boer War, cavalry survived only as ‘mounted infantry’ — troops who rode to the fight, dismounted and used rifles — rather than as a shock arm.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the industrial production of weapons in nineteenth-century Britain.

• Government armouries such as the Royal Small Arms Factory at Enfield Lock used steam-driven machine tools to mass-produce rifles with interchangeable parts.

lessons.title: Waterloo 1815 and Balaclava 1854: leadership, technology and reporting

before.content_html:
Two Battles, Forty Years Apart

Waterloo (18 June 1815) and Balaclava (25 October 1854) frame an extraordinary period of change. Waterloo was the climax of the Napoleonic Wars, fought with smoothbore muskets and disciplined squares of red-coated infantry. Balaclava was an early action of the Crimean War, fought as rifling, the telegraph and the camera were entering the battlefield. The two battles let us trace continuity (the bravery of the British soldier, the importance of leadership) and change (long-range weapons, public scrutiny, the rise of the war reporter).

Key Fact

At Waterloo (1815) the Duke of Wellington defeated Napoleon using infantry squares and disciplined defence on the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge. At Balaclava (1854) Lord Raglan’s vague order led to the doomed Charge of the Light Brigade.

Waterloo, 18 June 1815 — Wellington’s Defensive Masterpiece

Wellington positioned around 68,000 British, Dutch, Belgian and German troops along the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean, screened by walled farms (Hougoumont, La Haye Sainte and Papelotte). His plan was defensive: hold the ridge until the Prussians under Blücher could march from Wavre to attack Napoleon’s right flank. He used reverse-slope tactics — placing infantry just behind the crest so that French artillery could not easily target them, and so that French troops could not see the British until they crossed the ridge themselves.

When the French infantry square was tested. Massed French cavalry attacked uphill across boggy ground; the squares held under repeated charges, the cavalry could not break the bayonet wall, and French casualties mounted as British and KGL infantry kept up controlled volley fire. Wellington committed his last reserves only when the Imperial Guard finally advanced; the Guard, until that day undefeated, was thrown back at point-blank musket range. By dusk the Prussians had arrived in force on the French right and the army of Napoleon disintegrated.

The battle showed combined arms at maturity in the smoothbore era: infantry squares to defeat cavalry, cavalry counter-charges to break enemy infantry, and artillery to soften both. Wellington’s personal presence on the line, riding among his men under fire, mattered for morale at least as much as the formations themselves.

Balaclava, 25 October 1854 — Confusion and the Light Brigade

Forty years later British soldiers were still wearing red and obeying officers who had bought their commissions, but the battlefield itself had moved on. At Balaclava the Russians attacked the British supply port. The action produced three episodes that Britain remembers: the ‘Thin Red Line’ of the 93rd Highlanders, who repelled Russian cavalry without forming square; the Charge of the Heavy Brigade, which broke a much larger Russian cavalry force; and the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade.

The Light Brigade charge has become a case study in command failure. From his hilltop position Lord Raglan could see Russian infantry beginning to drag away captured British guns from the Causeway Heights. He sent Captain Nolan with a written order to recover the guns. Down on the valley floor, neither the cavalry commander Lord Lucan nor the brigade commander Lord Cardigan could see the same guns. When Lucan asked ‘What guns?’, Nolan made a sweeping gesture in the direction of the Russian artillery battery at the far end of the North Valley. The Light Brigade obeyed and rode straight at it. Nearly 700 horsemen rode into accurate Russian rifle, cannon and shell fire down a mile-long valley with batteries on three sides. Around 110 were killed and many more wounded; the brigade was effectively destroyed in twenty minutes.

The charge is famous, but it was one symptom of a wider problem. The Crimean army was supplied by horse-drawn carts on a few unmade tracks; thousands died of cholera, exposure and starvation in the winter of 1854–55. Officers had bought their commissions and many had no recent campaign experience. Russell’s reporting (see below) made all of this national news. The Crimean scandal forced the Cardwell reforms of 1868–74, which abolished the purchase of commissions and reorganised the army. Treat the Light Brigade as the visible peak of a structural Victorian problem, not a one-off mistake.

Why Outcomes Differed: Leadership and Technology

Comparing the two battles makes leadership the most visible variable. Wellington wrote orders that left no room for interpretation; he supervised key sectors personally. Raglan was at fault on multiple counts: from his hilltop he saw a different battlefield from the cavalry on the valley floor, his order was ambiguous, and Captain Nolan’s gesture made the misreading worse. The Russian commander Prince Menshikov was little better, but it was the British failures that mattered for the Light Brigade.

Technology had also moved. By 1854 the British infantry carried the Pattern 1853 Enfield rifle, accurate to 600 yards. Russian field artillery was breech-loading and rifled. The Light Brigade was a mounted unit attempting to ride a mile down a valley dominated by industrial-era weapons; the same charge in 1815 against smoothbore guns at the same range would have lost far fewer men. The Crimean War foreshadowed the killing power of industrialised weapons that would dominate the second half of the nineteenth century.

A New Public: Russell, Fenton and the Reading Nation

What made Balaclava different from any earlier British battle was that the public knew. William Howard Russell filed dispatches for The Times via the new electric telegraph, often within days of events. His report on the Light Brigade (‘some hideous blunder’) reached London while the wounded were still being treated. The photographer Roger Fenton was sent out under government sponsorship in 1855 to take posed photographs of officers and camp life; technical limits meant he could not photograph battle, but his images circulated as engravings in newspapers. Within months, ordinary middle-class Britons were reading and looking at war as an ongoing news event — not a finished story.

The result was a permanent change in the relationship between army and public. Florence Nightingale’s nursing mission was launched in direct response to Russell’s reporting on hospital conditions at Scutari. Parliament debated supply failures while the war was still being fought. By the Boer War of 1899–1902, war reporting was an established profession, photographs accompanied articles and concentration-camp policy became a national scandal. The press did not just describe wars: it began to shape them.

Key Fact

The Crimean War was the first British war to be reported by telegraph and photographed for publication. William Howard Russell of The Times exposed supply failures and battlefield blunders within days; this triggered Florence Nightingale’s nursing mission and, eventually, the Cardwell reforms.

1850s wet-plate photography needed exposures of several seconds and a portable darkroom in a horse-drawn van — useless for action shots. Fenton’s images therefore show camp life, parked artillery, and his own ‘Valley of the Shadow of Death’ (a Crimean ravine littered with cannonballs). The photographs framed war as a managed, dignified British project — arguably a kind of early photographic reportage shaped by official sponsorship. They are still useful as evidence, but examiners reward students who can weigh provenance (a government-sponsored photographer in 1855) against content.

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 16 marks for the historical content, plus up to 4 SPaG marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of historical terminology.

Indicative content — arguments for leadership as decisive:
• Wellington wrote precise orders, used reverse-slope tactics on the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge and was personally present along the line.
• Raglan’s order at Balaclava was ambiguous; from his hilltop he saw a different battlefield from his cavalry; Captain Nolan’s gesture compounded the error.
• Wellington committed reserves at the right moment (against the Imperial Guard); Raglan failed to recall the Light Brigade in time.

Indicative content — arguments for other factors:
• Weapons had changed: by 1854 rifled small arms and breech-loading artillery made a frontal mounted charge far more lethal than it had been at Waterloo.
• Terrain: Wellington chose his ground, fortified Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte; the Light Brigade rode a mile down a valley with Russian guns on three sides.
• Allied support: the Prussians arrived at Waterloo and tipped the battle; at Balaclava no equivalent reinforcement existed.
• Communications: in 1815 a commander’s eye and aide-de-camp were everything; by 1854 the telegraph and the press meant blunders became national news within days — sharpening the political consequences of poor leadership.
• Wider supply: the Crimean army was hungry, ill-supplied and stricken with cholera (Russell exposed this) — structural problems no Raglan-on-his-best-day could have erased.

Emerging: Limited argument with little period detail; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors.

lessons.title: Cardwell, professionalisation and the Victorian citizen-soldier

before.content_html:
Why Reform Came — The Crimean Aftermath

The Crimean War (1854–56) had been a strategic British victory but a public-relations disaster. William Howard Russell’s telegraphed reports for The Times had told Victorian readers about cholera in the trenches around Sevastopol, frostbitten soldiers without boots, and elderly officers who had bought their commands. Florence Nightingale’s mission to Scutari hospital exposed conditions inside the army’s own care system. By the late 1860s the political consensus was that Britain needed an army fit for industrial war.

Key Fact

Between 1868 and 1874 Edward Cardwell, Gladstone’s Secretary of State for War, abolished the purchase of officer commissions, introduced short service for soldiers, linked battalions to county districts and built recruitment depots.

Ending the Purchase System

The most striking change came in 1871. Until then, becoming an officer in most British infantry and cavalry regiments meant buying the rank. A second lieutenant’s commission cost £450; a lieutenant-colonel’s could exceed £7,000 — many years of an ordinary worker’s wages. Promotion was bought, not earned. The system filled the officer corps with wealthy gentlemen, some excellent and some, like the elderly commanders mocked by Russell, dangerously out of date. Cardwell pushed the abolition of purchase of commissions through Parliament against fierce resistance from the Lords. When the Lords blocked the bill, Gladstone had Queen Victoria abolish purchase by royal warrant. From 1871 promotion was based on seniority and merit, opening the officer corps to the middle class.

Short Service and Linked Battalions

Before Cardwell, soldiers signed on for at least 12 years — effectively a career. Recruits were often men with no other option and the army earned a reputation in respectable Victorian society for drink and disorder. The 1870 Army Enlistment Act introduced short service: six years with the regulars and six in the reserve. A young man could now leave the army with a working life still ahead of him; reservists could be recalled to the colours in an emergency, giving Britain a trained pool without the cost of a large standing army.

The 1872 Localisation Act paired infantry battalions in a linked battalion system: each regiment had two regular battalions, one serving overseas while the other recruited and trained at home in a fixed regimental district. The 1881 Childers reforms (which extended Cardwell’s framework) gave most regiments their now-familiar county titles — Royal Welch Fusiliers, Yorkshire Regiment, Royal Sussex Regiment. Recruitment depots in places like Lichfield (Staffordshire) and Pontefract (Yorkshire) became visible local institutions.

A More Professional Soldier

All of this fed a new image: the regular Victorian soldier as a professional, identifiable by his county regiment and his short-service contract. The popular nickname Tommy Atkins took hold during the late nineteenth century, especially through Rudyard Kipling’s 1892 poem ‘Tommy’. Pay improved modestly, conditions in barracks were standardised, and basic literacy classes ran in many depots. The Victorian regular was no longer to be a man written off as a drunkard; he was to be the steady, disciplined backbone of an empire-defending professional force.

The Cardwell reforms were a turning point, but they did not invent the modern army on their own. Earlier nineteenth-century commissions had already trimmed flogging and improved barracks; the Childers reforms of 1881 finished the regimental reorganisation; the Haldane reforms of 1906–12 created the Territorial Force, the modern General Staff and the British Expeditionary Force. Professionalisation was a thirty-year arc from c1868 to c1908. Examiners reward students who can show the chain of reform rather than treating Cardwell as a single moment.

Civilians, Recruitment and Requisitioning

In the eighteenth century the Royal Navy had relied on press gangs — men dragged from quaysides to fill ships’ crews. The army had used recruiting parties offering shillings and beer in market towns, while in wartime governments had requisitioned horses, wagons and lodgings for soldiers from villages along the line of march. Civilians had no formal protection from these demands.

By the second half of the nineteenth century the picture had changed. The end of impressment after 1815, expanding rail networks, and Cardwell’s recruitment depots meant the army recruited through visible local institutions instead of bullying tactics. Requisitioning became a managed transaction settled through county magistrates and quartermasters. The professional regular still came overwhelmingly from the urban poor — pay was low and the work hard — but the army was no longer extracting men and goods by force in the way it had once done.

Officers had paid real money for their commissions and treated them as property — the price of a colonelcy could be a family’s pension. The House of Lords contained many serving and retired officers and rejected the abolition bill. Gladstone’s government dared a constitutional confrontation by having Queen Victoria sign a royal warrant abolishing purchase, simply by removing the underlying authority that allowed officers to charge for their ranks. The Lords backed down, but resentment lingered for a generation. The episode shows how reform of the army was inseparable from wider Victorian arguments about class, merit and the constitution.

Press, Photography and Public Opinion

Cardwell’s reforms could not have happened without the press. Russell’s Crimean dispatches and the engravings worked up from Roger Fenton’s photographs had created a politically active public opinion that demanded change. By the time of the Boer War (1899–1902) the press cycle was even faster: photographs accompanied articles, the new mass-circulation papers (Daily Mail from 1896) reached millions, and concentration-camp policy in South Africa became a national scandal. The Victorian and Edwardian army professionalised in part because it was now visible to a literate, politically engaged nation that would not stand for a repeat of the Crimean shambles.

Key Fact

Cardwell’s reforms (1868–74) responded to a political climate created by press reporting. Russell of The Times exposed Crimean failures by telegraph; mass-circulation Victorian newspapers turned army reform into a national issue.

lessons.title: The Western Front and the Somme 1916

before.content_html:
The Industrialised Battlefield, 1914–18

By August 1914 the firepower of an industrial army made open-order assault almost impossible. Quick-firing artillery threw shells across miles of countryside; magazine-fed bolt-action rifles reached out 1,000 yards; and the machine gun could fire 500 rounds a minute. After the German advance was halted at the Marne, both sides dug in. From the North Sea to the Swiss border ran two parallel lines of trench system — with reserve trenches, dugouts, communication trenches and barbed-wire belts in between.

Key Fact

By the end of 1914 the Western Front had become a fortified line some 450 miles long. Quick-firing artillery, machine guns, magazine rifles and barbed wire gave the defender an overwhelming advantage; this is the technical reason the war ground into trench stalemate.

A New Composition of the Army

The pre-war British Expeditionary Force was a small professional army, the legacy of Cardwell and Haldane. It could not fight a continental war on its own. Lord Kitchener appealed for volunteers and within months hundreds of thousands had enlisted into the ‘New Armies’. From January 1916 the Military Service Act introduced compulsory conscription. By 1916 the army included specialised logistics corps, signal companies, tunnelling units, gas regiments, and from 1917 specialised tank battalions. The 1916–18 BEF looks much more like a modern army than its 1914 predecessor.

New Weapons on the Western Front

The technologies that would shape twentieth-century war all appeared, in working form, between 1914 and 1918. Chemical weapons (chlorine, phosgene and from 1917 mustard gas) inflicted casualties but rarely produced breakthroughs once gas-masks became standard. Aircraft began the war as scouts and ended it as bombers and fighters; the Royal Flying Corps merged with the Royal Naval Air Service in 1918 to form the Royal Air Force. Tanks — British secret weapon — first appeared on the Somme on 15 September 1916 (Flers-Courcelette) but were too few and unreliable to break the line; by Cambrai (November 1917) and Amiens (August 1918) they had matured into a battle-winning weapon.

Artillery remained the king of the Western Front. By 1916 a planned barrage could throw a million shells onto a small sector. The British army developed the creeping barrage, a moving curtain of shells that lifted in timed steps just ahead of the advancing infantry. When it worked — as on parts of 1 July 1916 and across the 1918 Hundred Days — it was lethal. When the timing slipped or the wire was uncut, infantry walked into machine-gun fire alone.

The Somme, 1 July–18 November 1916

The Somme was Britain’s first attempt at a continental-scale offensive. The plan, agreed with the French, was to break the German line on a 25-mile front north and south of the river Somme. After a seven-day artillery bombardment, on 1 July 1916 BEF infantry advanced over no man’s land. Hopes that the bombardment would have destroyed the German wire and dugouts proved badly misplaced — many German positions were intact, much of the wire was uncut, and the British timetable assumed troops would walk forward in lines. The result was the costliest day in British military history: roughly 57,470 casualties, of whom 19,240 were killed.

The Somme then ground on for over four months. Tactics evolved week by week: small-unit infiltration, better integration of infantry and artillery, the first use of tanks at Flers-Courcelette in September. By 18 November, when the offensive ended in mud and snow, the Allies had advanced perhaps 6–8 miles in places. Total Allied casualties exceeded 600,000; German casualties are estimated at 450,000–500,000. The Somme had killed huge numbers of soldiers without producing a strategic breakthrough — the textbook definition of a war of attrition.

The phrase ‘lions led by donkeys’ was popularised in Alan Clark’s 1961 book and the 1960s satirical revue ‘Oh! What a Lovely War’. Revisionist scholars from the 1990s onwards (Gary Sheffield, William Philpott, Dan Todman) argue this is a 1960s cultural verdict, not a 1916 one. They point to the BEF’s 1916–18 operational learning curve: the creeping barrage refined, tanks integrated, sound-ranging and counter-battery fire developed, infantry platoons reorganised around Lewis guns and bombers. By August 1918, BEF formations could break German lines as they did during the Hundred Days. Examiners reward students who can present both views and judge between them rather than recycle the ‘donkeys’ line.

The Role of General Sir Douglas Haig

Haig is the figure on whom the wider Somme debate turns. Critical case: he ordered the bombardment that did not cut the wire; he allowed the assault to proceed on 1 July despite mounting evidence the bombardment had under-performed in places; he sustained the offensive for over four months at terrible cost. Defensive case: Haig was fighting a coalition war that required Britain to take pressure off Verdun, where the French were close to collapse; the Somme bled the German army even more than it bled the BEF; the operational lessons learned in 1916 were applied in the 1918 victories that ended the war.

No serious historian today defends the first day of the Somme. The disagreement is over whether Haig should be judged by 1 July 1916, by 18 November 1916, or by 11 November 1918. The fairest answer probably weighs all three; in any event, the question is one of evidence and emphasis, not heroes and villains.

Several causes combined. The seven-day bombardment dispersed shells along too wide a front, much of it shrapnel that did not destroy concrete dugouts or cut deep barbed-wire belts. Many shells were duds (British munitions quality was still poor in early 1916). The advance plan assumed troops would walk forward in evenly spaced lines, partly because most New Army battalions were inexperienced and could not yet manage small-unit fire-and-movement. When the bombardment lifted, German machine-gunners climbed out of intact dugouts and opened fire across uncut wire. Whole battalions were destroyed in minutes. The day’s casualties — around 57,470 — remain the costliest in British military history.

Key Fact

The Somme cost roughly 600,000 Allied and 450,000–500,000 German casualties. By 1918 the BEF had absorbed the lessons — refined creeping barrages, infiltration tactics, tanks, counter-battery fire — and broke the German line in the Hundred Days offensive (August–November 1918).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of trench warfare on the Western Front.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a feature; a further mark for adding a supporting detail.

Indicative content (any two):
• A network of front-line, support and reserve trenches, connected by communication trenches running back from the line.
• Front-line trenches were typically 6–8 feet deep, lined with sandbags and reinforced with wooden duckboards and dugouts.
• Belts of barbed wire were laid in deep zigzag rows in front of the front line to break up infantry assaults and channel attackers into machine-gun fire.
• No man’s land — the exposed strip between the opposing front lines, typically 200–400 yards wide — was swept by machine-gun fire and laced with shell craters.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate, specific support.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to trenches without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the first day of the Somme (1 July 1916) was so costly for the British army.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The seven-day preliminary bombardment failed to destroy German dugouts or cut the deep belts of barbed wire on much of the front; many British shells were duds.
• The advance plan assumed New Army battalions would walk forward in evenly spaced lines, partly because they were inexperienced and could not yet manage small-unit fire-and-movement.
• When the bombardment lifted, German machine-gunners climbed out of intact concrete dugouts and opened sustained fire across uncut wire and exposed no man’s land.
• The British army was attempting its first continental-scale offensive with a largely volunteer New Army that had been raised in 1914–15; experience of combined-arms attack was limited.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (bombardment failure, dugouts, uncut wire, line-walking advance, New Armies) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the first day without explaining the cost.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of new weapons on the Western Front, 1914–18.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• Belt-fed machine guns such as the Vickers and the German Maxim could fire 400–600 rounds per minute, dominating the defensive role on no man’s land.
• Tanks first appeared on the Somme at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916, but were too few and unreliable to break the line until Cambrai (1917) and Amiens (1918).
• Chemical weapons (chlorine from 1915, phosgene and mustard gas from 1917) inflicted casualties but rarely produced strategic breakthroughs once gas-masks became standard issue.
• Aircraft began the war as scouts and ended it as fighters and bombers; the Royal Flying Corps merged with the RNAS in 1918 to form the Royal Air Force.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to WW1 weapons without identifying a feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Western Front became a war of attrition by the end of 1914.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of two or more reasons, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Quick-firing artillery and machine guns gave the defender an overwhelming advantage, making open-order assault costly and breakthroughs almost impossible.
• After the German advance was halted at the Marne (September 1914), both sides dug in, extending parallel trench systems from the North Sea to the Swiss border.
• Belts of barbed wire and concrete dugouts protected each side’s positions; once these defences were in place, frontal attacks could only succeed at huge cost in lives and shells.
• Strategic geography — flat northern France and Belgium, narrow front, no flanks to turn — meant neither side could manoeuvre around the other; the only way forward was through.

Mastering: Two reasons sustained with specific period detail (Marne, machine guns, barbed wire, no flanks) and explicit links to the question.
Secure: Two reasons explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified with limited detail.
Emerging: General comment that the war was bloody without explaining attrition.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of General Sir Douglas Haig at the Somme in 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• As commander-in-chief of the British Expeditionary Force he planned and ordered the Somme offensive in coordination with the French.
• He authorised the seven-day preliminary artillery bombardment that was intended to destroy German wire and dugouts before the infantry advance.
• He sustained the offensive for over four months from 1 July to 18 November 1916, despite the costly first-day casualties.
• He authorised the first operational use of tanks at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916, even though tank numbers and reliability were limited.

Mastering: Two features identified with accurate supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with brief support.
Developing: One feature with support, or two features named without support.
Emerging: Vague reference to Haig without identifying a feature.
